A spokesperson from the NHL tells me that the league’s highest-performing content includes both Celebrini and Smith, a duo many have nicknamed Willmack. The league is doubling down on the wider romance-fantasy of it all too: In late September, it launched “Hot for Hockey,” an audio series of short, fictional love stories based on real NHL players.

Celebrini and Smith are kind of inseparable, but in staged instances—interviews or social clips—they can seem a little guarded or awkward. In a recent clip, they’re seen promoting an “elevated cupcake experience,” which was a charitable meet-and-greet for which a fan paid $17,000. The most liked comment beneath this video, which was uploaded by the bakery behind the cupcakes, reads: “this looks like a hostage video they send to families for ransom.” Another earlier post has them stiffly “doing a spin” in New York City for the social media personality Judi Jupiter, who then calls the two “perfect specimens.” (Of hockey players’ famed physiques, Celebrini—trying on jeans for the shoot at Tech CU Arena—put it plainly: “Hockey butts…they make everything smaller.”) When I ask which of his and Smith’s antics haven’t yet made it online, he, almost defensively, says, “What do you mean? What do you want?” But then softens: “When we’re on the road, and we go to a sauna or steam room kind of place, you’re supposed to be quiet. If we walk into a sauna, it’s like, we start crying-laughing.”

The NHL’s chief marketing officer, Sean Eggert, says Celebrini “has quickly become one of our most visible players on and off the ice.” But even in this, he cites a clip of Celebrini and Smith that the league posted on TikTok in March of this year, referring to it as the “besties video.” In it, Celebrini is seen patiently calling Smith over during a game, with a slight and knowing smirk. Someone else’s voice is laid on top (a common trend on TikTok) saying, “Psst, hey, come here, cooooome here.” When Smith appears in the frame, the voice says, “Yaaaay.” “That was an inflection point,” says Eggert. It has millions of views.

blocks.c: Macklin Celebrini sitting on a workout bench

blocks.x: Celebrini alone is the NHL’s most popular athlete across its channels, says Eggert. Content focused on him generated north of 235 million views last season. But it’s not just that Celebrini is drawing numbers online; he’s also bringing in new viewers. Around 77% of the people who watched the “besties video” were women or girls—a figure Eggert says is “unprecedented, and disproportionate to the majority of content we put out there.” The NHL adds that most of Celebrini’s nearly 800,000 Instagram followers are female.

For his part, Celebrini—who has a public and verified Instagram account and a TikTok handle he keeps private—stays pretty mum on the subject. “I’ve had things sent to me,” he says. “I see a little bit of the content that people make.” But his algorithms only show him himself “once in a while,” he says. I ask him: “What do you think of all that? The narratives people might spin, and the fan fiction element?”
“I don’t really think about it,” he says, lowering his eyes and quieting his voice a little, seemingly ready to move on to another topic.
https://media.gq.com/photos/6ac3d7ee3ac76e582fa7ba93/4:5/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Macklin-Celebrini-WM-Web-2.jpg
https://media.gq.com/photos/6ac3cda8bd9b6edac82a6f00/4:5/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Macklin-Celebrini-WM-Web-5.jpg
blocks.c: Macklin Celebrini wearing his hockey uniform

blocks.x: Smith will tell me, via a voice note, that “out of the rink, [Mack] is just a normal kid” who “likes to have fun.” Now that we’ve been around each other all afternoon and dinner is about to wrap, he’s loosened a bit, and I can see the easygoing nature Smith described.

In the brief hours of each day that Celebrini doesn’t dedicate to hockey, he has a few peripheral hobbies. He plays Wiffle ball in his yard with his buddies. The Office is his favorite TV show, and he thinks The Odyssey is “unbelievable, maybe one of the best movies ever.” He loves Drake and he loves country music—fairly standard fare for a 20-year-old.

In other words, Celebrini is prodigious on the ice and is a “normal kid” off it. Such characters aren’t new in hockey, but few before him have found themselves so close to the center of a pop culture phenomenon. The NHL has always had big names, but it has not had a Gen Z personality whose fan base spans diehard hockey buffs to TikTokers who are just discovering the sport, yet might never go to a hockey game. For now, it seems, Celebrini is only selectively engaging with the latter, humoring the NHL’s desire to build his fan base without letting it bleed into how he approaches his day job. He’s far more interested in racking up goals than followers. But given his capability, his age, his looks, his concurrent rise with hockey’s broader appeal and its ascent in the conversation, he’s the sport’s runaway breakout. And the only way to go is up.

Our plates have been cleared, and Celebrini is tired. But he’s polite until the end. “I don’t want to leave you high and dry,” he says, “but I think I’m going to get going.” His house is five minutes away; I half-expect Smith to show up in the borrowed Range Rover to get him. But no. So, out at the curb, one of the most valuable and adept young players in hockey stands unbothered in the half-light, waiting for his Uber, as any 20-year-old might at closing time.

We have a really connected team…and I’ve felt that since day one.” He later adds: “I believe, and our team believes, in wanting to build something special.”

Celebrini and I are situated at a window table at the restaurant in Los Gatos. He orders three carne asada tacos—“no onion and no cilantro”—and a glass of water. Nearby, a father whispers in his daughter’s ear, she looks over and smiles, then picks up her phone to type something furiously.

Celebrini’s fame began with his talent, but it has been amplified by two major pop culture phenomenons: Heated Rivalry, a fictional gay hockey love story, and Off Campus, a fictional straight hockey-centric love story. These shows made a lot of watchers either hungry for love or horny (or both) and primed to look for those things within a hockey arena. Soon, spectators who’d never before been to a hockey game were filling the stands, making TikToks about “the boy aquarium” (a nickname for the rink). DJs at games began playing big needle-drop songs from Heated Rivalry—namely “I’ll Believe in Anything” by Wolf Parade and a cover of “All the Things She Said” by t.A.T.u.—to loud cheers. As it were, both Heated Rivalry and Off Campus actually started as books; the former was written by Rachel Reid, who once noted on her website that though her central characters, Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov, are not based on anyone specifically, the “extremely entertaining rivalry between Crosby and [the player Alexander] Ovechkin” was one of her “inspirations.”

Celebrini is a hot topic within this runoff fandom. Especially given said audience’s clear fascination with his and Smith’s relationship. Celebrini says their friendship grew out of a mutual need to maintain a semblance of normalcy (Smith, 21, also left college early). “A lot of the older guys have kids and stuff,” says Celebrini. “We were the only ones looking to do stuff after practice, so we were just always hanging out.” They are both squarely in a highly online age demo, and their dynamic is a double-tap magnet for both people who find it heartwarming that such a platonic relationship exists in the hypermasculine world of hockey and those who ship (romantically endorse) the two. A spokesperson from the NHL tells me that the league’s highest-performing content includes both Celebrini and Smith, a duo many have nicknamed Willmack. The league is doubling down on the wider romance-fantasy of it all too: In late September, it launched “Hot for Hockey,” an audio series of short, fictional love stories based on real NHL players.

Celebrini and Smith are kind of inseparable, but in staged instances—interviews or social clips—they can seem a little guarded or awkward. In a recent clip, they’re seen promoting an “elevated cupcake experience,” which was a charitable meet-and-greet for which a fan paid $17,000. The most liked comment beneath this video, which was uploaded by the bakery behind the cupcakes, reads: “this looks like a hostage video they send to families for ransom.” Another earlier post has them stiffly “doing a spin” in New York City for the social media personality Judi Jupiter, who then calls the two “perfect specimens.” (Of hockey players’ famed physiques, Celebrini—trying on jeans for the shoot at Tech CU Arena—put it plainly: “Hockey butts…they make everything smaller.”) When I ask which of his and Smith’s antics haven’t yet made it online, he, almost defensively, says, “What do you mean? What do you want?” But then softens: “When we’re on the road, and we go to a sauna or steam room kind of place, you’re supposed to be quiet. If we walk into a sauna, it’s like, we start crying-laughing.”

The NHL’s chief marketing officer, Sean Eggert, says Celebrini “has quickly become one of our most visible players on and off the ice.” But even in this, he cites a clip of Celebrini and Smith that the league posted on TikTok in March of this year, referring to it as the “besties video.” In it, Celebrini is seen patiently calling Smith over during a game, with a slight and knowing smirk. Someone else’s voice is laid on top (a common trend on TikTok) saying, “Psst, hey, come here, cooooome here.” When Smith appears in the frame, the voice says, “Yaaaay.” “That was an inflection point,” says Eggert. It has millions of views.

Celebrini alone is the NHL’s most popular athlete across its channels, says Eggert. Content focused on him generated north of 235 million views last season. But it’s not just that Celebrini is drawing numbers online; he’s also bringing in new viewers. Around 77% of the people who watched the “besties video” were women or girls—a figure Eggert says is “unprecedented, and disproportionate to the majority of content we put out there.” The NHL adds that most of Celebrini’s nearly 800,000 Instagram followers are female.

For his part, Celebrini—who has a public and verified Instagram account and a TikTok handle he keeps private—stays pretty mum on the subject. “I’ve had things sent to me,” he says. “I see a little bit of the content that people make.” But his algorithms only show him himself “once in a while,” he says. I ask him: “What do you think of all that? The narratives people might spin, and the fan fiction element?”

“I don’t really think about it,” he says, lowering his eyes and quieting his voice a little, seemingly ready to move on to another topic.

Smith will tell me, via a voice note, that “out of the rink, [Mack] is just a normal kid” who “likes to have fun.” Now that we’ve been around each other all afternoon and dinner is about to wrap, he’s loosened a bit, and I can see the easygoing nature Smith described.

In the brief hours of each day that Celebrini doesn’t dedicate to hockey, he has a few peripheral hobbies. He plays Wiffle ball in his yard with his buddies. The Office is his favorite TV show, and he thinks The Odyssey is “unbelievable, maybe one of the best movies ever.” He loves Drake and he loves country music—fairly standard fare for a 20-year-old.

In other words, Celebrini is prodigious on the ice and is a “normal kid” off it. Such characters aren’t new in hockey, but few before him have found themselves so close to the center of a pop culture phenomenon. The NHL has always had big names, but it has not had a Gen Z personality whose fan base spans diehard hockey buffs to TikTokers who are just discovering the sport, yet might never go to a hockey game. For now, it seems, Celebrini is only selectively engaging with the latter, humoring the NHL’s desire to build his fan base without letting it bleed into how he approaches his day job. He’s far more interested in racking up goals than followers. But given his capability, his age, his looks, his concurrent rise with hockey’s broader appeal and its ascent in the conversation, he’s the sport’s runaway breakout. And the only way to go is up.

Our plates have been cleared, and Celebrini is tired. But he’s polite until the end. “I don’t want to leave you high and dry,” he says, “but I think I’m going to get going.” His house is five minutes away; I half-expect Smith to show up in the borrowed Range Rover to get him. But no. So, out at the curb, one of the most valuable and adept young players in hockey stands unbothered in the half-light, waiting for his Uber, as any 20-year-old might at closing time.
